original_title: An explosive Lanterns still stays stubbornly grounded in character

en.title: Lanterns' Grounded Approach Divides Fans, But Character Depth Shines
en.summary: Despite cosmic expectations, HBO's Lanterns opts for a gritty, street-level mystery. Even comic legend Grant Morrison weighs in on the show's deliberate departure from its high-flying source material.
en.body:
The halfway point of HBO's **Lanterns** season 1 presents a crucial moment: accepting the series for what it is, and perhaps more importantly, for what it has consciously chosen *not* to be. While many fans might have anticipated a universe-spanning epic, **Lanterns** has instead delivered a deliberately low-key, Earth-bound superhero tale steeped in mystery and noir. This divergence from the high-flying, cosmic adventures typically associated with Green Lantern has, understandably, stirred conversation.

Even **Grant Morrison**, a formidable authority in the DC Comics realm, has offered their perspective. Initially drawn to the series by a perceived slight from co-creator **Damon Lindelof** regarding traditional superhero spectacle, Morrison ultimately provided a mixed but largely positive review. They lauded the performances of **Aaron Pierre** and particularly **Kyle Chandler**, though they confessed that Chandler's portrayal of Hal Jordan felt like a character they didn't quite recognize, quipping that he was more akin to "Dr. McCoy." Morrison's primary critique, echoing sentiments from a portion of the fanbase, centers on the show's fundamental structural choice: why adapt one of DC's most cosmically scaled franchises into a decidedly terrestrial, effects-light series? As Morrison aptly puts it, "DC has a ton of 'ground level' heroes... so why take this low-fi route with a franchise that should be competing with Star Trek or Star Wars?"

This question has permeated the early episodes, where ring-slinging is sparse and **Kyle Chandler's** Hal Jordan is depicted as someone almost embarrassed by his past heroic exploits, having basked in adulation for so long. A pivotal scene sees **John Stewart** dutifully fetching Hal's Lantern, only to discover one of Hal's long-mothballed Green Lantern suits packed away. This moment encapsulates the central conflict: John, groomed from birth for the Green Lantern mantle, is eager to embrace the extraordinary, while Hal, the current guardian of the Green, seems hesitant to fully step back into the role.

## The Fan Divide:

This narrative choice has inevitably created a schism among the **Lanterns** viewership. While some appreciate the show's commitment to character-driven drama and its unique take on the superhero genre, others lament the perceived lack of cosmic scope and the sparse utilization of iconic Green Lantern imagery and powers. The series is executive-produced by **Chris Mundy**, **Damon Lindelof**, and **Tom King**, a trio known for their nuanced storytelling, and the visible influence of their respective styles is undeniable. For those who value intricate plotting and compelling character arcs over bombastic action, **Lanterns** is a deeply satisfying mystery. However, for fans who yearned for a direct translation of the comic's grand scale, the show's grounded approach might feel like a missed opportunity.

## What's Next for the Lanterns:

As **Lanterns** continues its first season on HBO, the narrative momentum is building. Viewers can anticipate further exploration of the central mystery, the deepening of the complex relationship between Hal Jordan and John Stewart, and potentially, a gradual escalation of the stakes. The show's creators have expressed a desire to craft a compelling season, and the future hinges on whether this unique blend of noir and superheroics can continue to resonate with its audience, potentially earning a second season to further illuminate the path of the Green Lantern Corps.

This week, no greater comics authority than Grant Morrison* chimed in on Lanterns , offering up a mixed but leaning-positive review of this deliberately low-key superhero tale. Morrison, lured to watch by their annoyance over statements from co-creator Damon Lindelof seemingly mocking the sort of slam-bang comic book elements that—let’s face it—many fans were hoping for, nonetheless had copious praise for Aaron Pierre and (especially) Kyle Chandler. (Even if they confessed that Chandler’s Hal, whom Morrison calls “Dr. McCoy,” “wasn’t any Hal Jordan [they] recognized.” Morrison’s main complaint, one shared by a moderate swath of the fan community, is a fundamental and structural one. Why turn Green Lantern—on of DC’s most high-flying, cosmically scaled comics universes—into a decidedly Earth-bound, occasionally dour, effects-skimpy street-level TV series? As Morrison states, “DC has a ton of ‘ground level’ heroes, or characters with low-level gimmick powers to choose from, so why take this low-fi route with a franchise that should be competing with Star Trek or Star Wars ?” It’s a question that’s been running through the series’ first three episodes, where ring-slinging is sparse and Chandler’s Jordan is portrayed as someone who’s been soaking in the adulation from his flashy, costumed heroics so long that he’s a little embarrassed by it. The scene where John dutifully fetches Hal’s Lantern only for Hal to see one of his long-mothballed Green Lantern suits packed in the same duffel bag gets at the central conflict ably. John, literally raised to be a Green Lantern, wants to get to the good stuff already, while the current keeper of the flame shies away from shining it on evildoers—or, indeed, at all. John, as Marine-straight and patiently impatient as he looms in Hal’s periphery, wants that ring— and that suit. His desire to help people is the one link he shares with his unwilling mentor, that unspoken tie holding John back from doing what Laura Linney’s Guardian grows more insistent each episode that he do and just taking the ring off of Hal Jordan’s finger. “The Weenie,” from its jokey title on down, tilts as close as Lanterns has gotten yet to the buddy-cop element overrepresented in the promotional materials.
